documents.prompt: A proposed solution to $\dfrac{x-{{p}}}{x-{{q}}}=0$ is $x={{q}}$. Why is the proposed solution invalid?
attemptFeedback: A rational equation is defined only where every original denominator is nonzero. Check candidate values in the original equation.
supportHints: A value can satisfy a simplified equation and still be invalid if it makes an original denominator zero.

solutionReview.headline: At $x={{q}}$ the denominator is 0, so the expression is undefined there.
reasoning: At $x={{q}}$ the denominator is ${{q}}-{{q}}=0$, and division by zero is undefined.
The real solution makes the numerator 0 instead: $x={{p}}$, where the denominator is ${{p}}-{{q}}={{pq}}$.
So $x={{q}}$ is invalid: It makes the denominator equal to zero.
solutionReview.commonError: Blaming the numerator: a zero numerator is what makes a fraction 0; a zero denominator makes it undefined.
solutionReview.answerSummary: It makes the denominator equal to zero.

documents.prompt: The equation $\dfrac{(x-{{p}})(x-{{q}})}{(x-{{q}})(x-{{r}})}=0$ is defined for all real $x$ except ${{q}}$ and ${{r}}$. What is its real solution?
attemptFeedback: A rational equation is defined only where every original denominator is nonzero. Check candidate values in the original equation.
supportHints: A value can satisfy a simplified equation and still be invalid if it makes an original denominator zero.

solutionReview.headline: The numerator is 0 at {{p}} and {{q}}, but {{q}} is excluded: $x={{p}}$.
reasoning: A fraction is 0 when its numerator is 0 and its denominator is not.
The numerator is 0 at $x={{p}}$ and at $x={{q}}$, but $x={{q}}$ also makes the denominator 0, so it is excluded.
At $x={{p}}$ the denominator is $({{p}}-{{q}})({{p}}-{{r}})={{den}}$, not 0. So the solution is $x={{p}}$.
solutionReview.commonError: Keeping $x={{q}}$: the expression is undefined there, even though the numerator is 0.
